title: Spectral Sequences And Applications
notes: Open by naming the chapter's organizing move: replace a large cohomology problem by a staged bookkeeping system. The lecture is an overview, so the goal is not to prove every convergence theorem. The goal is to make the page machine legible and then follow how filtered complexes, transgression, Gysin sequences, torsion, and rational models reuse the same small set of moves.

title: Chapter Roadmap
notes: Use the roadmap as a promise about continuity. Section 14 builds the algebraic machine, Section 15 reminds us why integer information matters, Section 16 gives the path fibration as the cleanest transgression laboratory, Sections 17 and 18 route the machine into homotopy theory, and Section 19 translates the rational part into Sullivan's differential graded algebra language.

title: Filtered Complexes Hide Layers
notes: Pause on the word filtered. A filtration is not extra decoration on a complex; it is a way of saying that some information is visible before other information. The differential respects the layers, so the associated graded object can be studied one slice at a time. The spectral sequence is the record of corrections as deeper interactions are allowed to appear.

title: Pages Are Successive Ledgers
notes: Frame an E-page as a ledger of provisional classes. The entries are not yet final cohomology classes; they are survivors at a particular resolution. Moving from E_r to E_{r+1} means taking cohomology with respect to d_r. That repeated operation is why the same grid can gradually remove classes that looked legitimate on earlier pages.

title: The Differential Has A Slope
notes: The bidegree rule is the first visual anchor: d_r: E_r^{p,q} -> E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}. For r equal to zero the arrow is vertical, for r equal to one it is horizontal, and later pages make longer diagonal jumps. Stress that the page number changes which bidegrees can communicate, which is exactly what later makes transgression visible.

title: Double Complexes Supply Pages
notes: Connect the filtered-complex abstraction to double complexes. A total differential combines vertical and horizontal pieces with signs chosen so D squared is zero. Filtering by columns or rows produces different early pages, but both are ways of interrogating the same total cohomology. This is the algebraic pattern behind Cech-de Rham and bundle examples.

title: Fiber Bundles Give A Geometric Page
notes: A fibration turns the page grid into geometry: one direction records the base and the other records the fiber. In favorable cases the E_2 page resembles H^p(B; H^q(F)), with local-system caveats suppressed for this overview. The important teaching point is that cohomology of the total space is assembled from base and fiber data plus differentials.

title: Transgression Is A Long Jump
notes: Introduce transgression as a class that survives the short differentials and then travels from the fiber direction into the base direction. The path fibration is perfect because the total path space is contractible. Positive-degree classes cannot survive forever, so a long differential must account for the disappearance and identify a base class with a fiber-originating class.

title: Path Fibration For Spheres
notes: In the sphere case, the clean cartoon is d_n from a loop-space generator in bidegree (0,n-1) to the base generator in bidegree (n,0). The formula is not offered as the full loop-space computation. It isolates the mechanism: contractibility of the total space forces a nonzero transgression, and that differential becomes information about the base.

title: Gysin Sequence As A Page Shadow
notes: Now turn the same page logic into a long exact sequence. For an oriented circle bundle over S^2, the only fiber rows are q equal to zero and one, so the decisive differential is d_2. It is multiplication by the Euler class. Varying the Euler number changes the matrix, and the survivors in total cohomology change accordingly.

title: Euler Class Controls Survivors
notes: Use the three-column sweep to make the Gysin statement concrete. When the Euler number is zero, the differential vanishes and product-like classes remain. When it is one, the map is an isomorphism over the integers and the middle cohomology disappears. When it is two, the cokernel records torsion. One differential explains three different total-space patterns.

title: Integer Coefficients Reveal Torsion
notes: The chapter does not stay only in de Rham territory because real differential forms cannot see all integral phenomena. A small cellular model, such as the RP^2 boundary map multiplied by two, reminds students that torsion is a cohomological feature, not a visual accident. Spectral sequences with integer coefficients can carry exactly this information through the page machine.

title: Applications To Homotopy Theory
notes: Read this as a dependency graph rather than a theorem dump. Path fibrations provide transgressions; Hurewicz relates first nontrivial homotopy to homology; Eilenberg-MacLane spaces isolate a single homotopy group; Postnikov and Whitehead towers assemble or remove layers. Spectral sequences provide the cohomological bridge that lets those constructions produce computable restrictions.

title: Rational Homotopy Compresses The Pattern
notes: Sullivan minimal models are introduced as a compression of rational homotopy information into a differential graded algebra. The odd sphere has one generator with zero differential. The even sphere needs a second generator whose differential kills a square. This mirrors the chapter's larger theme: the differential is not bookkeeping noise; it encodes the topology.

title: Chapter Synthesis
notes: Close by asking students to track three questions whenever a spectral sequence appears. What is filtered, what does each page entry mean, and which differential has the geometric interpretation? That habit makes the chapter's applications feel less scattered: transgression, Gysin sequences, torsion calculations, and rational models are different readings of the same filtered-complex grammar.
